title: From DevOps to Platform Engineering: A Roadmap Through Kubernetes, Terraform and CI/CD
description: What platform engineering is, how it grew out of DevOps, and a step-by-step learning roadmap through Linux, CI/CD, Terraform, Kubernetes, GitOps and developer portals.
body:
In the early days of DevOps, the message was simple: developers and operations should share ownership, automate everything and ship small changes often. As companies grew, that message ran into a practical problem. Asking every product team to master Kubernetes manifests, Terraform modules, cloud networking, security policies and observability tooling created enormous cognitive load and inconsistent results.

Platform engineering is the response. A platform team builds an internal developer platform: a set of self-service tools and paved paths that let product engineers create services, environments and pipelines safely without needing to be infrastructure experts. This guide explains the idea, then lays out a DevOps and platform engineering roadmap for students and junior engineers who want to work in DevOps, site reliability or platform roles.

## What platform engineering actually means

A useful way to think about it: the platform team treats infrastructure as a product, and other engineers are its customers. Typical platform capabilities include:

- **Golden paths:** templates for a new service that come with CI/CD, logging, monitoring, security scanning and deployment already wired up.
- **Self-service infrastructure:** request a database, queue or environment through a portal or a pull request rather than a ticket.
- **Developer portals:** a catalogue of services, owners, documentation and dependencies, often built with Backstage or a commercial alternative such as Port.
- **Guardrails:** policies enforced automatically (for example with Open Policy Agent or Kyverno) instead of manual reviews.
- **Shared observability:** standard metrics, logs and traces, often built on OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Grafana.

The goal is to make the right way the easy way.

## DevOps, SRE and platform engineering compared

| Role | Main focus | Typical work |
|---|---|---|
| DevOps engineer | Automation of build, test and deployment | CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code, environment management |
| Site reliability engineer | Reliability of production services | SLOs, incident response, capacity planning, toil reduction |
| Platform engineer | Internal tools that make other engineers productive | Developer portal, service templates, Kubernetes platform, self-service infra |

Titles overlap heavily, and many job postings mix all three. The core skills are shared, which is why the roadmap below works for each.

## The learning roadmap

### Stage 1: Linux, networking and scripting

Everything else sits on this foundation. Learn to work comfortably in a shell, manage processes and services, read logs, set file permissions and use SSH. Understand DNS, HTTP and HTTPS, TCP ports, load balancers and basic firewall rules. Write scripts in Bash, then pick up Python or Go for anything larger.

**Practice:** set up a Linux virtual machine, host a small web app behind Nginx with HTTPS, and automate the setup with a script.

### Stage 2: Git and CI/CD

Learn branching, pull requests and code review. Then build pipelines with **GitHub Actions** or GitLab CI that lint, test, build artifacts and deploy. Understand caching, secrets management in CI, and the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment.

**Practice:** add a pipeline to one of your projects that runs tests on every pull request and deploys on merge to the main branch.

### Stage 3: Containers

Learn to write efficient **Dockerfiles** (multi-stage builds, small base images, non-root users), run multi-container apps with Docker Compose, and push images to a registry. Understand image layers, tags and vulnerability scanning.

**Practice:** containerise a backend, database and frontend and run them together with one command.

### Stage 4: Infrastructure as code

Learn **Terraform** or **OpenTofu**: providers, resources, variables, outputs, modules and, critically, state. Understand remote state, locking and why you should never edit infrastructure by hand once it is managed as code. Learn at least one cloud provider's core services: compute, networking (VPCs, subnets, security groups), storage, IAM and managed databases.

**Practice:** provision a VPC, a small Kubernetes cluster or VM, and a managed database with Terraform, all from a GitHub repository with a plan-on-PR workflow.

### Stage 5: Kubernetes

Learn the core objects: Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and resource requests and limits. Then learn how to package apps with **Helm** or **Kustomize**, how health probes and rolling updates work, and how autoscaling behaves. Use a local cluster (kind, k3d or minikube) to experiment cheaply.

**Practice:** deploy your containerised app to a local cluster with health checks, an ingress and horizontal autoscaling.

### Stage 6: GitOps and observability

With **GitOps**, tools such as Argo CD or Flux continuously sync your cluster to the state declared in Git, so every change is reviewed and auditable. Pair it with observability: Prometheus for metrics, Grafana for dashboards, a logging stack and OpenTelemetry for traces. Learn to define simple SLOs and alerts.

**Practice:** manage your cluster's apps through Argo CD and build a Grafana dashboard with an alert for error rate.

### Stage 7: Platform thinking

Finally, put on the platform engineer's hat. Build a template that creates a new service with pipeline, Dockerfile, Helm chart and dashboards already set up. Register it in a Backstage catalogue. Add a policy that blocks containers running as root. Write documentation as if another team will use it, because that is the job.

## A capstone project for your portfolio

Combine the stages into one repository employers can review: Terraform for the cloud or local infrastructure, a Kubernetes cluster managed by Argo CD, two small services deployed through GitHub Actions, Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring, and a "create a new service" template. Document the architecture, the decisions and the trade-offs in the README. Our [GitHub portfolio guide for junior developers](/blog/github-portfolio-guide-junior-developers-hireable) covers how to present it.

## Common mistakes

- **Jumping straight to Kubernetes** without Linux, networking and containers. Debugging becomes guesswork.
- **Collecting certifications without projects.** Interviewers ask what you have built and broken.
- **Committing secrets** to repositories. Use secret managers and `.env.example` files from day one.
- **Ignoring cost.** Shut down cloud resources after experiments and set billing alerts.

## Next steps

Describe your capstone on a resume using the posting's language, then verify it with the free [ATS resume checker](/ats-checker). Browse [DevOps and cloud jobs](/jobs) and [remote roles](/remote-jobs) to see which tools appear most in the postings you care about, and prepare for the design rounds that often accompany these roles with our [system design interview guide](/blog/system-design-interview-primer-distributed-systems).

faq.a: Platform engineering is better seen as one way of putting DevOps ideas into practice at scale. Instead of every team managing its own infrastructure, a platform team builds shared, self-service tooling. DevOps culture, automation and shared ownership remain the foundation.

faq.q: Can a fresher get a DevOps or platform engineering job?
faq.a: Yes, though many teams prefer some software or operations experience. Freshers improve their chances with solid Linux and networking basics, a strong CI/CD and Kubernetes project, infrastructure as code on GitHub, and sometimes an entry-level cloud certification.

faq.q: Should I learn Docker before Kubernetes?
faq.a: Yes. Kubernetes runs containers, so you need to understand images, containers, networking and volumes first. Docker or another OCI-compatible tool is the natural starting point.

OpenTofu is an open-source fork of Terraform with largely compatible syntax. The concepts of providers, resources, state and modules transfer directly, so learning either one prepares you for both. Check which one your target employers mention.

faq.q: Are cloud certifications worth it for DevOps roles?
faq.a: An entry-level certification can help a resume pass screening, especially for freshers and career switchers. It is much stronger when paired with a public project that shows you can actually build and operate infrastructure.
